title: Fewest Presses on a Remappable Keypad
statement:
An old phone has 8 letter keys (the digits 2 to 9). You may assign the letters to keys however you like: each letter goes on exactly one key, a key can hold any number of letters, and you choose their order on the key. To type the letter in position p on its key (1 for the first), you press that key p times.

You get a string word whose letters are all different. Choose the assignment that makes typing word cheapest, and return the total number of key presses. Only letters that appear in word need a place.

examples.why: Put each letter first on its own key: 1 + 1 + 1.
Eight letters fill the first slot of all 8 keys for 1 press each. The other four go second on some key for 2 presses each: 8 + 8. The usual 3-letters-per-key phone layout is not required.
Eight letters cost 1, eight cost 2, eight cost 3, and the last two cost 4: 8 + 16 + 24 + 8.

constraints: word has only lowercase English letters, all different
hints: Every letter appears exactly once, so every letter matters equally. How many letters can cost only 1 press?
Only 8: one on the first slot of each key. The next 8 letters cost 2, the next 8 cost 3, and so on.
The i-th letter you place (counting from 0) costs ⌊i / 8⌋ + 1. Add that up, or use a closed form.

explain.intuition:
There are only 8 cheapest slots: the first position on each key. Then 8 slots that cost 2, then 8 that cost 3. Since every letter in the word appears once, each one adds exactly its slot cost, so the best you can do is fill the cheap slots first.

That gives a simple greedy: the letter you place as number i (from 0) costs ⌊i / 8⌋ + 1. Which letter goes where does not matter at all, only how many letters there are. If letters could repeat, you would give the cheap slots to the most frequent letters; here every frequency is 1.
steps: For i from 0 to n − 1, add ⌊i / 8⌋ + 1 to the total.
Return the total. In closed form: with f = ⌊n / 8⌋ full rounds and r = n mod 8 leftovers, the total is 8 · f(f + 1)/2 + r · (f + 1).
pitfalls: Assuming the standard layout of 3 or 4 letters per key. The mapping is yours to choose.
Using 9 or 10 keys. Only digits 2 to 9 carry letters, which is 8 keys.
Off by one in the cost: the 9th letter (index 8) costs 2, not 1.

solutions.title: Fill slots round by round
solutions.idea: Hand out letters to the cheapest free slot: 8 at cost 1, then 8 at cost 2, and so on.

solutions.title: Closed form
solutions.idea: f full rounds of 8 cost 8·(1 + … + f); the r leftover letters each cost f + 1.

followups: Letters can now repeat in the word. Which letters should get the cheap slots?
The phone has k letter keys instead of 8. What changes in the formula?
